summary:
We developed a digital interactive storybook that brings retired NASA missions to life through playable, educational experiences. Our digital storybook contains Opportunity, Ingenuity, and the Kepler Space Telescope, allowing users to explore each mission through storybook pages, interactive scenes, visuals, mission facts, and simple gameplay.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming information about retired NASA equipment into an experience that is easier and more engaging for children and casual space enthusiasts. Rather than only reading static facts, users can interact with the missions and learn through exploration and visual storytelling.

Our goal is to make space science more accessible, memorable, and enjoyable, while highlighting the discoveries and achievements of spacecraft whose missions may have ended but whose impact continues.
details:
Our project is a digital interactive storybook that combines storytelling, visuals, and simple gameplay to teach users about retired NASA missions in a more engaging way. The prototype features Opportunity, Ingenuity, and the Kepler Space Telescope, with each mission presented as its own interactive story.

Users can flip through storybook-style pages, explore mission-inspired environments, interact with objects, and discover educational facts as they progress. Instead of presenting information only as text, we wanted users to learn by actively participating in the story.

The project is mainly intended for children around ages 9–13 and casual space enthusiasts. Our goal is to make NASA mission history easier to understand, more memorable, and fun to explore.

We developed the interactive experiences using the Godot game engine and GDScript, with the project designed to run in browser on PC and mobile.

Creatively, we combined the familiar feel of a children’s storybook with interactive game elements. We focused on keeping the visuals playful, the controls simple, and the scientific information understandable without overwhelming younger users. We also considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, mobile/browser compatibility, and how to clearly separate real mission facts from artistic visualizations.
